summary: The paper introduces CODEC, which combines Integrated-Gradients-style contribution attribution at hidden layers with a sparse-autoencoder decomposition to expose 'contribution modes' — coordinated groups of neurons that causally drive network outputs. The framework is applied to ResNet-50, a retinal ganglion-cell CNN, and (briefly) ViT-B, producing findings about layerwise sparsity, positive/negative decorrelation, and effective mode-guided ablation/preservation, plus a promising neuroscience application to dynamic receptive fields. The direction is worthwhile and the retinal analysis is a genuine strength, but the method is an incremental step over prior contribution analyses (Tanaka 2019; Maheswaranathan 2023) plus standard SAE decomposition, and the empirical claims are undersupported by baselines, statistical evidence, and breadth of models.
strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: distinguishing receptive-field-like activation analyses from projective-field/causal contribution analyses is well argued and relevant to a growing interpretability audience.

Concrete causal validation via ablation/preservation experiments on ImageNet classes, with a fair comparison to activation-based modes (Fig. 6D–E) — this is the kind of intervention test many interpretability papers omit.

Novel and non-trivial application to a CNN model of retinal ganglion cells, tying contribution modes to dynamic receptive fields and to prior neuroscience results on population modes (Prentice 2016; Schnitzer & Meister 2003).
Empirical observations about layerwise sparsity growth, dimensionality increase, and progressive decorrelation of positive/negative contributions are interesting and non-obvious.
Reasonable robustness sweep over SAE hyperparameters (threshold, dictionary size, L1, seed) reported in supplement.

key_concerns.issue: Novelty is incremental. Applying Integrated Gradients to hidden neurons is explicitly credited to Tanaka (2019) and Maheswaranathan (2023); running a sparse autoencoder on the resulting per-image vectors is a direct transfer of standard SAE interpretability practice from activations to contributions. The paper does not clearly delineate what is conceptually new beyond this composition.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a dedicated Related Work section that (a) situates CODEC against contemporary SAE interpretability literature (e.g., Bricken et al., Cunningham et al., Marks & Tegmark, transcoders, attribution patching, Geiger-style causal abstractions) and (b) states precisely which findings/tools are new versus repurposed.

key_concerns.issue: Baseline coverage is thin. The only real comparison throughout is 'SAE on activations vs SAE on contributions.' Missing comparisons to attribution patching, path patching, activation patching / causal scrubbing, concept probing, TCAV, and prior circuit-discovery methods make it hard to claim CODEC is the right tool for causal interpretation.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add head-to-head experiments comparing mode-guided ablation/preservation efficacy against at least attribution patching and a probing baseline on the same ResNet-50 setup.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical soundness is not established. Fig. 3, 5, 6, 8 report single-number summaries (Hoyer index, FOEV, correlations, ablation curves, performance scores) with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests reported in the main text; the robustness sweep in supplement covers reconstruction R^2 but not the downstream interpretability metrics.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report seed variability for all main metrics (sparsity, decorrelation trajectory, class-correlation histograms, ablation/preservation curves) and confidence intervals on the block-6-to-7 transition claim.

key_concerns.issue: Generality claims outrun evidence. The paper is titled and framed as a general framework for causal interpretation of neural networks, but the CNN evidence is essentially ResNet-50 only, the ViT analysis is one paragraph acknowledging worse ablation, and LLM analysis is deferred to supplement. The retinal model is a 3-layer CNN, not 'state-of-the-art' in the general sense.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either add substantive results on a second CNN architecture (e.g., ConvNeXt, EfficientNet) and expand the ViT results (with an analysis of why ablation is weaker), or scope the claims to 'sensory feedforward CNNs and their biological analogues.'

key_concerns.issue: Sparse autoencoder design is under-specified and under-motivated. The encoder is only referred to as 'an encoder network f_enc' and 'MLP size'; the decision to use sigmoid+hard-threshold rather than TopK/JumpReLU/L1 SAEs (now standard in interpretability) is not justified, and no comparison against modern SAE variants is given. Non-negativity is imposed on D but signed contributions are decomposed — the interaction is not discussed.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Fully specify the encoder architecture, motivate the threshold-sigmoid choice against contemporary SAE variants, and include an ablation swapping in a TopK/JumpReLU SAE.

key_concerns.issue: The contribution-target reduction (top-1 logit) is a strong scalarization choice that could bias what 'causal' means; alternatives are mentioned but not compared.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Show how much mode structure and downstream perturbation results depend on top-1 vs top-k vs entropy targets.

key_concerns.issue: Several typographical and grammatical issues (e.g., 'retinl', 'selecte channels', 'non-labled', 'discrimiate') and multiple mis-spacings in the main text.

The mode-guided input visualization (Fig. 7) is presented mostly qualitatively; without a quantitative evaluation (e.g., pointing-game, human eval, insertion/deletion metrics), it is hard to assess claims that modes capture reusable semantic components across classes.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a quantitative visualization metric (e.g., insertion/deletion AUC or class-consistency of mode-highlighted regions across images).

questions_for_authors: How does CODEC compare quantitatively to attribution patching / activation patching for causal channel identification on the same ablation/preservation task?

How sensitive are the reported layerwise trajectories (sparsity, positive/negative decorrelation, dimensionality) to the choice of contribution target and to the attribution method (IG vs SmoothGrad vs ActGrad)?
For the ViT results, is the weaker ablation performance a limitation of CODEC or of treating tokens as spatial dimensions? Can you isolate this with an alternative token/channel treatment?
How does an SAE trained directly on activations but then evaluated via contribution-space projection compare to CODEC? This would help disentangle 'SAE gains' from 'contribution-space gains.'

For the retinal application, do contribution modes give better predictions or interpretations than existing methods (e.g., NMF on interneuron responses, or the analyses in Maheswaranathan et al. 2023)?
Why non-negative D combined with signed c? Do you effectively split each mode into +/- pairs, and if so, how does this interact with the reported decorrelation of positive/negative contributions?

Are the ablation/preservation improvements over activation-based modes statistically significant across seeds and classes, and does the block-6-to-7 transition survive multiple-comparisons correction?
calibration_check: Claims about layerwise trends, decorrelation, and ablation efficacy are well-scoped to the ResNet-50 evidence, but the framing as a general interpretability framework and the phrase 'state-of-the-art models of neural activity in the vertebrate retina' overreach relative to the actual experiments (one CNN backbone plus a 3-layer retinal model, with ViT/LLM largely deferred).

significance.justification: Contribution-space decomposition is a useful lens and the retinal findings are genuinely interesting, but the ANN findings largely re-express things visible via existing attribution + SAE tooling.

novelty.justification: The two building blocks (IG at hidden layers; SAE decomposition) are prior art; the specific composition, the surprisal target for the retinal model, and the mode-guided ablation protocol are the main new pieces.

rigor.justification: Method is described at a reasonable level and completeness-of-IG is exploited soundly, but SAE architecture is under-specified, and several methodological choices (target scalarization, non-negative D with signed c) are not justified.

statistical_soundness.justification: Main-text figures report point estimates without seed variance, error bars, or significance tests; the important qualitative claims (layerwise transitions, class-correlation gains, ablation curves) lack statistical backing.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations section acknowledges the ResNet-only main analysis and the weaker ViT results, but title/abstract framing as a general causal-interpretation framework is somewhat overclaimed.

clarity.justification: The conceptual picture is communicated well and captions are informative, but the writing has many typos and spacing issues and some methods paragraphs (SAE architecture, InputGrad) are dense and under-specified.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard sectioning is present in spirit but Related Work is folded into the intro and the paper lacks a dedicated experimental setup section, which is unusual for ICLR.

reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters (threshold, dictionary size, epochs, batch, learning rate, L1 scale) and training compute are stated, and the datasets/models are public benchmarks, but encoder architecture, exact scalarization defaults per experiment, and randomization protocols are only partly specified.

related_work.justification: Contemporary SAE interpretability literature and modern circuit-discovery / activation-patching methods are essentially absent from the positioning; comparison largely stops at Grad-CAM/SmoothGrad/IG and the two cited retinal papers.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe eight figures that clearly map onto specific claims (pipeline, layerwise stats, SAE schematic, mode-class correspondence, ablation/preservation, input visualization, retinal IRFs), supporting rather than decorating the narrative.

breadth_generality.justification: The paper frames CODEC as a general framework, but the main evidence is one CNN (ResNet-50) plus a 3-layer retinal CNN; ViT is one paragraph with weaker results and LLMs are deferred to supplement.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline reject: promising direction and one strong application, but incremental novelty, thin baselines, weak statistical reporting, and overreaching generality push it below the ICLR bar as submitted.
